outlooks.summary: Scattered to isolated severe storms are possible from the upper Great Lakes region southwestward into the mid Missouri Valley and central Plains. A few strong to severe storms with gusty winds and hail are possible over the northern Rockies as well as west Texas. A few strong storms with gusty winds are also possible from east Texas into the lower Mississippi Valley region.

sections.title: Synopsis
sections.text: Shortwave trough currently moving through the Great Lakes will continue northeast into southeastern Canada this morning. In wake of this feature, general high rises will occur within belt of modest westerlies from the central through northern Plains. Weak vorticity maxima embedded within this zone of flow will play a role in thunderstorm initiation this afternoon. Surface low associated with the northern-stream shortwave trough will occlude over Ontario. Trailing front will extend southwest through MN into southwestern NE this morning. This front will advance southeast during the day and likely extend from northeast WI through IA and southern NE where it will stall near the KS border. A dryline will stretch from west TX through northwest KS where it will intersect the front. ...Central Plains through the middle Missouri Valley and upper Great Lakes... Rich low-level moisture with upper 60s to 70 F dewpoints will advect northward through the pre-frontal warm sector and into the central Plains and middle MO Valley region beneath steep mid-level lapse rates. sections.title: West Texas
sections.text: Isolated to widely scattered storms are expected to develop along the dryline across west TX by late afternoon. Winds aloft will continue to decrease resulting in weak shear as heights rise during the day. However, the thermodynamic environment with steep lapse rates and moderate instability will support a risk for downburst winds and hail through early evening.

sections.title: Northern Rockies through central High Plains
sections.text: At least isolated storms will likely develop over the northern Rockies and spread east into the high Plains where 45+ kt effective bulk shear will support potential for some supercell structures. Moisture will be limited and storms will be high based, but will pose a risk for downburst winds and large hail. Activity might consolidate into one or two small clusters overnight. A slight risk might be needed for a portion of this region in later updates, most likely from western NE into western SD and northeast WY. ..Dial/Cook.. 06/25/2019

outlooks.summary: The greatest potential for severe thunderstorms today is over parts of the central Plains to northern Missouri, where very large, destructive hail and sporadic severe gusts are possible.

sections.title: Synopsis
sections.text: Pattern evolution in mid/upper levels this period will include a pronounced cyclone digging southeastward offshore from the Pacific Northwest, and downstream mean-ridge amplification across the Rockies and High Plains. Weak perturbations are evident in moisture-channel imagery over western OR and southwestern ID; these should move through the mean ridge position toward the northern Great Plains this afternoon into tonight. Meanwhile, the sharply amplified, negatively tilted trough now over northwestern ON, Lake Superior and Lake Huron will redevelop a closed 500-mb low and move north-northeastward toward the ON Hudson Bay shoreline. In the southern stream, a weak but still prominent trough in moisture-channel imagery over south TX -- with one or two associated MCVs -- will move slowly east-northeastward to northeastward over southeast TX and LA. Associated large-scale lift aloft and low- level mass response will support scattered to numerous thunderstorms across parts of the lower Sabine, Arklatex and lower Delta regions today, with potential for embedded/damaging wet downbursts. sections.title: Central Plains to upper Great Lakes
sections.text: Scattered, episodic thunderstorms are expected to develop over the outlook area this afternoon and evening, near the baroclinic zone and east of the dryline. The main concern will be severe hail -- some significant and destructive at 2+ inches in diameter. Severe gusts also are possible, along with a couple tornadoes. The frontal zone should be the main focus for convective development as the increasingly high-theta-e warm sector -- the inflow sector for surface-based convection -- destabilizes substantially this afternoon. With moist advection throughout the day, mid 60s to near 70s surface dew points already observed upstream in southern/central OK, and diurnal evapotranspiration in the region, moisture should be more than adequate for afternoon/evening severe potential. Seasonally cold midlevel temperatures are expected -- e.g. 500-mb values close to -14 deg C -- part of a favorable thermodynamic profile featuring steep low/middle-level lapse rates and a deep troposphere. Resulting MLCAPE values of 2500-3500 J/kg should be common, locally exceeding 4000 J/kg. sections.title: North-central High Plains
sections.text: Isolated to widely scattered thunderstorms should develop this afternoon, with initiation possible over higher terrain of northern WY, extreme southern MT and the Black Hills, and from the surface low along a weak trough/convergence zone near the western border of SD. Any sustained convection will be in a favorable vertical wind profile to become supercellular with large hail and severe gusts -- the main question being one of coverage. Between the threat for a couple afternoon supercells over western SD and additional evening activity moving out of northeastern WY, the cumulative coverage of severe potential now appears to justify a 15%/slight area. Though mid/upper heights will be rising through the day as the synoptic ridge amplifies, the aforementioned perturbations over the Northwest may provide regionally enhanced large-scale ascent/ destabilization in support of convective potential. A low-level moisture/theta-e axis should extend from the NE Sandhills northwestward across the Badlands/Black Hills region, combining with afternoon insolation to support a corridor of weak MLCINH and MLCAPE in the 1000-1500 J/kg range, atop a well-mixed, high-lapse-rate boundary layer. outlooks.summary: The greatest potential for severe thunderstorms today is over parts of the central Plains to northern Missouri and southern Iowa, where very large hail and sporadic severe gusts are possible.

sections.title: NE/KS/MO/IA
sections.text: Water vapor imagery shows relatively strong zonal midlevel winds extending from the northern Great Basin across the northern Plains. The southern fringe of the stronger westerlies lies across CO/KS/MO, where a weak E-W surface boundary is also present. South of the boundary, southerly low-level winds are helping to transport very moist air northward, with dewpoints expected to approach 70F by late afternoon along the border of eastern KS/NE. Strong heating is also occurring, which will yield an extremely unstable air mass. Present indications are that isolated intense storms will form along the boundary in the 19-21z period, with initial supercells capable of very large hail and damaging wind gusts. An isolated tornado or two is also possible. Activity is expected to build quickly eastward during the late afternoon along the boundary into southern IA and northern MO. Activity may organize into one or more short bowing segments with a risk of damaging wind gusts.

sections.title: Northern Plains
sections.text: The axis of strong midlevel winds extends across southern MT into SD, with a few weak shortwave troughs embedded in the flow. It appears likely that widely scattered strong storms will develop over the higher terrain of western and southern MT by late afternoon - spreading eastward through the evening. As this activity emerges into western SD later today, slightly greater moisture/instability profiles may result in sufficient intensification for a few organized severe storms capable of large hail and damaging winds.

sections.title: IA/IL/WI into Lower MI and northern IN
sections.text: Morning visible satellite imagery shows a well-defined MCV over eastern IA. Strong heating is occurring ahead of this feature, and some of the 12z CAM guidance suggests that a cluster of thunderstorms will intensify this afternoon over southern WI/northern IL. If this occurs, strong westerly flow aloft, steep low-level lapse rates, and sufficient CAPE would pose a risk of damaging wind gusts. Have expanded the risk areas slightly farther east/south into Lower Michigan and northern Indiana, and will monitor the region for further expansions of severe potential in later updates. ..Hart/Goss.. 06/25/2019

outlooks.summary: The greatest potential for severe thunderstorms this afternoon into the evening is forecast from southeast Nebraska to northwest Missouri and southern Iowa, where very large hail and sporadic severe gusts are possible.

sections.title: Discussion
sections.text: The only substantial change this forecast update was to trend towards the notion of greater storm coverage across parts of southeast NE east along the MO/IA border. Short-term guidance has shown a tendency for lower storm coverage across parts of east-central KS where 30-percent hail probabilities were located in the previous outlook. Have adjusted these probabilities to both communicate this trend in model guidance but also to seemingly reflect where convective potential appears highest across southeast NE according to visible satellite imagery. Otherwise, the previous forecast thinking is on track. ..Smith.. 06/25/2019 .PREV DISCUSSION... /ISSUED 1102 AM CDT Tue Jun 25 2019/

mesoscale_discussions.summary: Isolated severe thunderstorms with a damaging wind and hail risk may develop this afternoon. Severe Thunderstorm Watch issuance is possible depending on radar trends.
mesoscale_discussions.discussion: A well-defined MCV that originated from convection earlier this morning across NE will continue moving quickly eastward around 40 kt along the WI/IL border this afternoon. Low-level airmass recovery is still underway to the east of this MCV, with the environment only weakly unstable. But, surface dewpoints have generally increased into the upper 50s and lower 60s across north-central/northeastern IL. Recent VWP profiles from KDVN and KLOT show strong westerly flow around 35-50 kt in the 2-4 km AGL layer in association with the MCV. There is some concern that as low-level lapse rates continue to steepen, some of these enhanced winds aloft could reach the surface if a small thunderstorm complex can develop. Radar imagery from 18Z shows a recent increase in reflectivity along the WI/IL border, and this could be the first attempt at the formation of a bowing segment. Isolated strong to damaging winds appear to be the main threat, although hail could occur in the strongest updrafts as mid-level lapse rates gradually steepen. Although watch issuance is not immediately likely, an increase in convective coverage/intensity may warrant a Severe Thunderstorm Watch at some point this afternoon.

mesoscale_discussions.summary: Severe risk is gradually increasing, with storm initiation expected within the next hour or so. WW will likely be required.
mesoscale_discussions.discussion: Latest surface analysis shows a surface baroclinic zone arcing from southern Nebraska east/east-northeastward across southern and eastern Iowa at this time. Near and south of this front, diurnal heating of a boundary layer featuring dewpoints in the 60s, combined with steep lapse rates aloft (as sampled by 18Z DDC special RAOB) is yielding moderate destabilization along and south of the boundary. Visible satellite imagery shows subtle increases in cu development in a few areas -- mainly along the surface front over southern Nebraska, and near the remnant MCV moving across central Kansas. Isolated storms are expected to initiate in one or both of these areas in the next 1-2 hours or so, and then spread eastward into Iowa -- and possibly northwestern Missouri. Initial, cellular storm mode is expected, favoring large hail -- and possibly a tornado where surface winds are backed near the front. With time, some upscale growth may occur, which could support an uptick in wind risk, mainly east of the Missouri Valley. We will continue to monitor cu field evolution, with an eye toward WW issuance -- likely prior to 4 PM.

mesoscale_discussions.summary: Isolated to scattered storm development is occurring across the southern high Plains. Isolated stronger storms may be accompanied by local severe risk, but WW issuance is not expected at this time.
mesoscale_discussions.discussion: Latest visible satellite imagery shows continued CU-field development across the southern High Plains, where heating of a modestly moist boundary layer has yielded some destabilization. Several CBs are indicated over the Davis Mountains vicinity, but weak flow here, and northward into southeast New Mexico and the Texas South Plains area, suggests only limited/isolated severe risk. Farther north, and axis of greater low-level moisture lingers across portions of the Texas Panhandle, which is supporting greater CAPE development. Though flow aloft is generally weak, the slightly enhanced flow as compared to areas farther south -- combined with the greater low-level moisture and CAPE -- suggests that risk for severe weather is a bit greater across this portion of the discussion area. Still, at this time, WW issuance is not expected in the short term, though we will continue to monitor the region over the next couple of hours.

mesoscale_discussions.summary: Isolated strong/gusty winds may occur with storms spreading eastward this afternoon and evening. Watch issuance is unlikely.
mesoscale_discussions.discussion: Strong westerly flow is present across the northern Rockies and High Plains this afternoon, with 45-50 kt estimated around 6 km AGL per KBLX VWP. Low-level moisture remains quite limited however, with generally 40s surface dewpoints observed across southern MT into parts of northern WY. Still, a deeply mixed boundary layer should encourage efficient downdraft accelerations with any convection that forms over higher terrain and which subsequently spreads eastward this afternoon and evening. Isolated strong/gusty winds may occur given the strength of the flow aloft, but weak instability (MLCAPE around 250-500 J/kg) will likely temper a greater severe risk. Marginally severe hail may also occur with the strongest updrafts. Overall severe threat appears isolated/marginal, and watch issuance is unlikely at this time.

mesoscale_discussions.summary: An isolated severe threat is expected to continue from far eastern Wyoming eastward across southwestern South Dakota and northwestern Nebraska early this evening. Hail and damaging wind gusts will be the primary threat. Weather watch issuance can not be ruled out.
mesoscale_discussions.discussion: Latest surface analysis shows a 1005 mb low over central Wyoming with a corridor of maximized low-level moisture from central Nebraska into southwestern South Dakota, where an axis of low-end moderate instability is analyzed. MLCAPE values are in the 1000 to 1500 J/kg according to the RAP. Isolated severe storms are ongoing to the west of Rapid City and northeast of Cheyenne. These storms should continue to move eastward across the High Plains and will interact with stronger instability. In addition, regional WSR-88D VWPs show 40 to 50 kt of 0-6 km shear suggesting the environment will support supercells. Any storm that rotates could produce isolated large hail. Wind damage will also be possible. The need for weather watch issuance will likely be determined by storm coverage early this evening.

mesoscale_discussions.summary: A severe threat is likely to continue from southeast Nebraska into southern Iowa over the next few hours. The threat should also increase across northeast Kansas. Large hail and wind damage will be the primary threats. Trends will continue to be monitored for possible watch issuance across parts of north-central and northeast Kansas.
mesoscale_discussions.discussion: Latest water vapor imagery shows a west-northwest mid-level flow pattern over the central Plains with mid-level moisture streaming eastward from Wyoming and northern Colorado into Nebraska. Thunderstorms are located along the southern edge of the plume from southern Nebraska into southern Iowa. A moist airmass is located to the south of this convection with surface dewpoints in the mid 60s F and MLCAPE values estimated int he 2000 to 3000 J/kg range. In addition, the Hastings and Omaha WSR-88D VWPs have 35 to 40 kt of 0-6 km shear suggesting supercell development will continue to take place this evening. Large hail and wind damage will be possible with the stronger cells. The severe threat should affect northern Kansas and northwest Missouri as cells move east-southeastward into those areas later this evening.

mesoscale_discussions.summary: The severe threat continues across remaining portions of WW 443.
mesoscale_discussions.discussion: An MCS has crossed southern Lake Michigan recently, with a couple of severe storms located along its southern flank across far southwestern Michigan and far northwestern Indiana. These storms are progressing into gradually weaker instability with eastward extent, with the ongoing severe threat expected to decrease over time in tandem with boundary layer cooling. Farther west, a low-level boundary extends from near Chicago southwestward to near PIA. Although towering cumulus were noted with this boundary, subtle subsidence aloft in the wake of a mid-level wave east of the region was likely limiting convective development along this boundary. With boundary layer cooling expected to lead to stabilization through the remainder of the evening, western portions of WW 443 may be cancelled early. An upcoming Watch Status message will reflect these evolving convective trends. ..Cook.. 06/25/2019 ...Please see www.spc.noaa.gov for graphic product...

mesoscale_discussions.summary: A linear complex has evolved over far northeastern Kansas. A new Severe Thunderstorm Watch and/or spatial/temporal extensions to ongoing WW 444 are possible.
mesoscale_discussions.discussion: Earlier storms over south-central Nebraska has evolved into a linear complex while migrating southeastward into far northeastern Kansas. These storms have exhibited better organization that high-resolution models have suggested, and have began to forward-propagate while producing gusty winds and 1-1.25 inch hail stones. These storms are also on the southern end of WW 444, and a reservoir of strong instability (4000+ J/kg MUCAPE) resides just ahead of the storms across the discussion area. It is uncertain how far southeast these storms will persist given weak shear aloft, although the current presentation of the storms and the modest strengthening of southerly low-level flow (to around 20-25 kts) suggests that storms may persist beyond the southern extent of WW 444 and cross I-70 over the next 1-2 hours. If these storms do hold together, either a new WW issuance or spatial/temporal extensions of WW 444 will be needed to address the threat.

mesoscale_discussions.summary: A severe threat is expected to continue across WW 445 and may spread eastward across central Illinois over the next 1 to 2 hours. Wind damage and hail will be the primary threats. A WW extension may be needed across parts of central Illinois as the storms move eastward toward the edge of the watch.
mesoscale_discussions.discussion: A cluster of strong to severe thunderstorms is ongoing in western Illinois, located along the northern edge of a moist airmass with surface dewpoints in the lower to mid 60s F. This is contributing to low-end moderate instability across central Illinois with the RAP estimating MLCAPE values in the 1000 to 1500 J/kg range. In addition, the Lincoln WSR-88D VWP shows 0-6 km shear of 35-40 kt with veered south-southwesterly winds at the surface. 40 kt of westerly flow is evident near 3 km AGL which is likely being enhanced by a speed max at 700 mb over southern Iowa. This should be enough continue a severe threat as the storms move across central Illinois over the next few hours. Wind damage would be the primary threat although hail could also occur with the stronger updrafts.

mesoscale_discussions.summary: Hail remains possible over WW 446 in Iowa, but is expected to wane over the next couple hours. Farther west, additional marginal hail or wind is expected to develop across eastern Nebraska.
mesoscale_discussions.discussion: Cells continue to redevelop near the warm front in southwest IA where southwest 850 mb winds continue to feed elevated moisture and instability into the cluster. To the south, an MCS has recently moved south across eastern Kansas, producing a large pocket of relatively stable outflow air. It is possible that the pocket of instability supporting the IA storms will begin to stabilize as air advects northeastward out of KS. West of the IA activity, new storms have formed over southeast NE, on the northwest periphery of the stable air where southwest 850 mb winds are able to maintain a northeastward advection of unstable air. A similar situation may thus persist over southeast NE with multiple cores capable of hail over the next few hours. Northwest of there, a small MCS with distinct outflow boundary is rapidly moving east across north-central NE. As this outflow encounters the zone of warm/moist air advection, it too will have a chance at increasing in intensity, with hail or wind possible. If upward convective trends persist, a watch may need to be considered for eastern NE. ..Jewell.. 06/26/2019 ...Please see www.spc.noaa.gov for graphic product...

mesoscale_discussions.summary: A few strong wind gusts or marginal hail remains possible across the watch area. Additional watches are not expected at this time.
mesoscale_discussions.discussion: The primary outflow surge continues to turn more southward, now approaching the KS border. Local radar shows outflow well ahead of this line which has a history of strong to marginally severe gusts. Behind the outflow, an extensive area of elevated storms persists northwestward toward ONL. These storms have shown hail potential at times, but in general have been decreasing in intensity as of late. While winds off the surface remain southwesterly, and the air mass unstable, the strongest lift from warm advection appears to be over. In addition, height rises will continue into the day. As a result, the weakening trend is expected to continue, and additional watches are not anticipated for this regime. ..Jewell.. 06/26/2019 ...Please see www.spc.noaa.gov for graphic product...
